cases.n: Westchester County grand jury — Archdiocese of New York (2002)
cases.place: White Plains, Westchester County, New York
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of New York
cases.cover: Grand jury called the church's handling of complaints 'an orchestrated effort to protect abusing clergy members from investigation, arrest and prosecution'
cases.d: A Westchester County grand jury issued a 13-page report in June 2002 after a two-month inquiry that reviewed tens of thousands of pages of archdiocesan documents and heard from eight alleged victims. It found the church's handling of abuse claims was an orchestrated effort to shield abusing clergy from investigation and prosecution. It recommended making it a felony for church officials not to report allegations and ending the statute of limitations for crimes against minors. The archdiocese called the report unfair.
cases.cite: Westchester County Grand Jury report, June 2002, as reported by CBS News / AP, 20 June 2002

cases.n: Suffolk County grand jury — Diocese of Rockville Centre (2003)
cases.place: Rockville Centre, Long Island, New York
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Rockville Centre
cases.cover: Accused priests moved from parish to parish; a diocesan 'intervention team' and legal-affairs team used to silence victims and suppress claims; secret archives on 43 priests
cases.d: A Suffolk County grand jury report presented by District Attorney Thomas Spota in February 2003, after a nine-month investigation, found that at least 58 abusive priests had been protected by the Diocese of Rockville Centre. Officials used sham policies and an 'intervention team' that silenced victims, moved abusers between parishes where they had access to children, and ignored treatment advice. The grand jury said the failures could not be put down to incompetence. No one was charged because of the statute of limitations.
cases.cite: Suffolk County Supplementary Grand Jury report, February 2003, as reported by The Irish Times, 13 February 2003

cases.n: New Hampshire Attorney General — Diocese of Manchester (2003)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Manchester
cases.cover: Diocese chose to protect itself and its priests; lenient treatment of accused priests; false statements in civil suits alleged; diocese acknowledged evidence 'likely to sustain a conviction' in a December 2002 agreement that avoided indictment
cases.d: On 3 March 2003 the New Hampshire Attorney General released a 154-page report, with about 9,000 pages of church records, after a 10-month investigation. It found 50 priests credibly accused of abusing minors over 60 years and said the diocese showed 'flagrant indifference' to the danger to children. Under a December 2002 agreement the diocese avoided criminal charges for child endangerment, acknowledged evidence likely to sustain a conviction, and accepted annual monitoring by the Attorney General for at least five years.
cases.cite: New Hampshire Attorney General, Report on the Investigation of the Diocese of Manchester, 3 March 2003, as reported by The Boston Globe, 4 March 2003

cases.n: Maine Attorney General — Diocese of Portland (2004)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Portland (Maine)
cases.cover: Church officials kept abuse complaints secret and reassigned at least seven accused priests to parishes; one was later accused of abusing at least 10 girls
cases.d: In February 2004 the Maine Attorney General reported on allegations reaching back 75 years against 63 men: diocesan priests, members of religious orders and church or school employees. The report found that church officials kept abuse charges secret and reassigned some accused priests, placing children at risk. No accusations of abuse after 1996 were found, and no one could be charged because of the statute of limitations.
cases.cite: Maine Attorney General report on the Diocese of Portland, February 2004, as reported by the Portland Press Herald, 25 February 2004

cases.n: Philadelphia grand jury — Archdiocese of Philadelphia (2005)
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia
cases.victims_note: 'Hundreds' of minors, per the grand jury
cases.cover: Grand jury found Cardinals John Krol and Anthony Bevilacqua knew of the abuse and covered it up; the archdiocese disputes this
cases.d: A Philadelphia grand jury released a 418-page report in September 2005 finding that at least 63 priests of the archdiocese had abused hundreds of minors over several decades. It found that Cardinals John Krol and Anthony Bevilacqua knew of the abuse and concealed it. No charges were brought because most cases fell outside the time limit for prosecution.
cases.cite: Report of the County Investigating Grand Jury, Philadelphia, 21 September 2005, as reported by JURIST

cases.n: Second Philadelphia grand jury — priests still in ministry (2011)
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Philadelphia
cases.cover: A senior archdiocesan official was charged with moving priests with abuse complaints to new parishes without warning; up to 37 priests with credible allegations remained in ministry
cases.d: A second Philadelphia grand jury reported in February 2011 that as many as 37 priests remained in active ministry despite credible allegations of sexual abuse. The two-year investigation led to charges against two priests, a former priest and a Catholic school teacher, and against Monsignor William Lynn, the archdiocese's former secretary for clergy, accused of transferring problem priests without warning parishes. The archdiocese then suspended 21 priests named in the report.
cases.cite: Report of the Grand Jury, Philadelphia, 21 January 2011 (released 10 February 2011), as reported by CBS News, 9 March 2011

cases.n: Pennsylvania grand jury — Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown (2016)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown
cases.cover: Two bishops concealed the abuse; the grand jury said the church had such sway over law enforcement that it helped select a police chief
cases.d: A statewide investigating grand jury, in a report released by the Pennsylvania Attorney General on 1 March 2016, found that more than 50 priests and religious leaders abused hundreds of children in the Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown over about 40 years. Two bishops, including Bishop Joseph Adamec, concealed the abuse. The report said the diocese had enough influence over local law enforcement to help choose a police chief.
cases.cite: Pennsylvania 37th Statewide Investigating Grand Jury, Report I, 1 March 2016, as reported by AP / The Columbian

cases.n: Colorado Attorney General special master — three Catholic dioceses (2019)
cases.who: Archdiocese of Denver; Dioceses of Colorado Springs and Pueblo
cases.cover: On average 19.5 years passed between a credible allegation and restricting the priest; more than half of victims were abused after the diocese already knew the priest was an abuser; euphemisms used in records
cases.d: A report by special master Bob Troyer, a former US Attorney appointed by Attorney General Phil Weiser, was released on 23 October 2019. It found that 43 priests sexually abused at least 166 children in Colorado's three Catholic dioceses over 70 years, most in the 1960s and 1970s. On average it took 19.5 years from a credible allegation to a restriction on the priest, and more than half the victims were abused after the church already knew of the priest. A supplemental report followed on 1 December 2020.
cases.cite: Special Master's Report on Colorado's Roman Catholic Dioceses, 22 October 2019, as reported by Colorado Public Radio, 23 October 2019

cases.n: Florida Office of Statewide Prosecution — Catholic clergy abuse (2020)
cases.who: Catholic dioceses of Florida
cases.cover: Florida was a state where accused priests were 'routinely relocated'; the report found acts by the church that enabled sexual abuse of minors
cases.d: Florida's Office of Statewide Prosecution closed a two-year investigation, opened after the 2018 Pennsylvania grand jury report, with a report released on 6 November 2020. It found historical sexual abuse allegations against 97 priests in Florida, none of whom could be prosecuted because of the statute of limitations, earlier prosecution or death. It found that accused priests had been routinely relocated and that church acts had enabled abuse of minors, but found no evidence of ongoing unreported abuse. More than 260 tips were received.
cases.cite: Office of Statewide Prosecution, Report on Sexual Abuse in the Catholic Church in Florida, 6 November 2020, as reported by ABC Action News / Tampa Bay 28

cases.n: St. Joseph's Orphanage, Burlington — Vermont task force (2020)
cases.who: St. Joseph's Orphanage, run with roles for the Catholic Diocese of Burlington, the Sisters of Providence and Vermont Catholic Charities
cases.cover: The Attorney General said police and prosecutors failed to investigate allegations when they were first made; the Sisters of Providence did not produce requested documents
cases.d: A task force of the Vermont Attorney General, Burlington's mayor, the Chittenden County State's Attorney, the Vermont State Police and Burlington police investigated former residents' allegations for two years after a 2018 BuzzFeed News report. Its report of about 300 pages, released on 14 December 2020, said 'it is clear abuse happened and children suffered', including physical and sexual abuse, but found too little evidence to prove alleged murders. Attorney General T.J. Donovan said police and prosecutors had failed to investigate complaints when first made; no charges were possible because of time limits.
cases.cite: St. Joseph's Orphanage Task Force report, 14 December 2020; Vermont Attorney General press release; WCAX, 14 December 2020

cases.n: Iowa Attorney General — clergy abuse review (2021)
cases.who: Archdiocese of Dubuque; Dioceses of Des Moines, Davenport and Sioux City; other faith leaders
cases.cover: Survivors told the Attorney General their allegations had been ignored or covered up by the church
cases.d: Iowa Attorney General Tom Miller's office released its review on 23 June 2021 after an inquiry begun in late 2018. It examined 50 complaints, 45 involving the Catholic Church, with records involving 70 priests and alleged abuse from the 1930s to 1997. It described an 'overwhelming' history of abuse and cover-ups but found the four dioceses had reformed in recent decades. No case could be prosecuted because of the statute of limitations.
cases.cite: Iowa Attorney General, Clergy Abuse Report, 23 June 2021, as reported by Iowa Public Radio

cases.n: Nebraska Attorney General — three Catholic dioceses (2021)
cases.who: Archdiocese of Omaha; Dioceses of Lincoln and Grand Island
cases.victims_note: 258 victims of sexual abuse; about 60% were minors at the time; the office said the count is incomplete
cases.cover: The church knew of the assaults and did not properly report them to law enforcement
cases.d: The Nebraska Attorney General's Office released a report on 4 November 2021 after a three-year investigation of the state's three Catholic dioceses. It identified 258 victims, nearly 60% of them minors at the time, and 57 abusers, with abuse dating back to the 1930s. It found that the church knew of assaults and failed to report them properly to law enforcement. No charges were possible because the statute of limitations had expired.
cases.cite: Nebraska Attorney General, Report on Catholic Church Sexual Abuse, 4 November 2021, as reported by Nebraska Public Media

cases.n: Kansas Bureau of Investigation — Catholic clergy abuse (2023)
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Kansas City in Kansas and other Kansas dioceses
cases.cover: The KBI found the church protected suspected clergy for decades, often by transferring priests to other churches; some victims were bound by non-disclosure agreements
cases.d: A four-year Kansas Bureau of Investigation inquiry, reported in January 2023, reviewed five decades of church records and identified 188 clergy suspected of crimes including rape and indecent liberties with a child. Investigators interviewed nearly 140 victims and witnesses in 15 states and referred 30 cases to prosecutors, all of which were too old to charge. The KBI found the church had protected these men for decades, often by moving them.
cases.cite: Kansas Bureau of Investigation summary report, January 2023, as reported by Kansas News Service / NPR (WFAE), 15 January 2023

cases.n: New York Attorney General v. Diocese of Buffalo (2020–2022)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Buffalo; retired Bishop Richard Malone and Auxiliary Bishop Edward Grosz
cases.cover: The Attorney General alleged diocesan leaders protected more than two dozen accused priests by not sending their cases to the Vatican
cases.d: In November 2020 the New York Attorney General sued the Diocese of Buffalo and its retired bishops, alleging that they protected more than two dozen priests accused of child sexual abuse. In a settlement filed on 25 October 2022 the diocese accepted enhanced child-protection measures and an independent compliance auditor, and the two bishops were barred from fiduciary roles in New York charities.
cases.cite: People of the State of New York v. Diocese of Buffalo, complaint 23 November 2020; stipulation of settlement 25 October 2022, as reported by America magazine

cases.n: New York Attorney General — Diocese of Brooklyn agreement (2024)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Brooklyn
cases.cover: The diocese did not consistently follow its own procedures, sometimes did not disclose credible allegations and did not monitor accused clergy; one priest was transferred between parishes for years after complaints
cases.d: On 16 April 2024 the New York Attorney General announced an agreement after finding that the Diocese of Brooklyn had failed to follow its own procedures for abuse complaints, applied inconsistent standards of proof and did not adequately monitor credibly accused clergy. In one case a priest who admitted repeatedly abusing minors stayed for years without parishioners being told; in another a priest was moved between parishes despite complaints from the 1990s onward. The diocese accepted new procedures and an independent monitor.
cases.cite: New York Attorney General, Assurance of Discontinuance with the Diocese of Brooklyn, 16 April 2024, as reported by Insurance Journal / AP

cases.n: Michigan Attorney General — diocese-by-diocese reports (2022–2026)
cases.who: Catholic Dioceses of Marquette, Gaylord, Kalamazoo, Lansing, Grand Rapids and Saginaw (Archdiocese of Detroit pending)
cases.d: After search warrants were executed at all seven Michigan dioceses in October 2018, the Attorney General's office published one report per diocese: Marquette (27 October 2022), Gaylord (8 January 2024), Kalamazoo (22 May 2024), Lansing (16 December 2024, 56 people accused, 48 of them priests), Grand Rapids (15 December 2025, 51 priests) and Saginaw (25 June 2026, 37 priests and one deacon). By June 2026 the investigation had received 1,276 tips, brought 11 criminal cases and obtained 9 convictions covering 38 survivors. The office states that inclusion in a report does not mean an allegation was substantiated.
cases.cite: Michigan Department of Attorney General press releases on the Dioceses of Grand Rapids (15 December 2025) and Saginaw (25 June 2026); CBS Detroit on Lansing (16 December 2024)

cases.n: Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia — Atlanta and Savannah (2023)
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of Atlanta; Diocese of Savannah
cases.cover: Some accused priests were reassigned without notice to officials at their new posts; historical church policies 'enabled sexual abuse of minors'
cases.d: A review by the Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia, dated 20 March 2023 and covering both dioceses that together span the whole state, found credible allegations of child sexual abuse against 28 priests while serving in Georgia, dating back to the 1940s. It found that some accused priests were reassigned without notice and that historical policies enabled abuse; Savannah began taking allegations seriously in the late 1980s and Atlanta in the 1990s. No case could be prosecuted.
cases.cite: Prosecuting Attorneys' Council of Georgia report, 20 March 2023, as reported by Catholic News Agency / EWTN News, 29 March 2023

cases.n: Rhode Island Attorney General — Diocese of Providence (2026)
cases.who: Catholic Diocese of Providence
cases.cover: The diocese kept abuse secret and failed to report it to civil authorities; under Bishops McVinney and Gelineau accused priests were moved or sent to 'treatment' and returned to ministry, where some abused again; the diocese refused in-person interviews
cases.d: Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha published a report on 4 March 2026 after an investigation begun in 2019. It identified 75 credibly accused clergy and more than 300 victims abused between 1950 and 2011. It found the diocese kept abuse secret, did not report it to civil authorities, and under Bishops Russell McVinney and Louis Gelineau moved accused priests or returned them to ministry after 'treatment'. Four current or former priests were charged during the investigation.
cases.cite: Rhode Island Attorney General, report on child sexual abuse in the Diocese of Providence, 4 March 2026 (press release)

cases.n: Massachusetts Attorney General — Worcester, Fall River and Springfield dioceses (2026)
cases.place: Boston, Massachusetts (Attorney General); dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield
cases.who: Catholic Dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield
cases.d: On 30 September 2026 the Massachusetts Attorney General's office released a report finding that more than 270 Catholic clergy abused nearly 1,000 children in the Dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield, with abuse dating back to the 1950s. It described institutional failures and recommended better investigation of allegations and more accurate records. It followed the Attorney General's 2003 report on the Archdiocese of Boston.
cases.cite: Massachusetts Attorney General report on the Fall River, Springfield and Worcester dioceses, 30 September 2026, as reported by WBUR

cases.n: Ramsey County v. Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis (2015–2016)
cases.who: Catholic Archdiocese of St. Paul and Minneapolis
cases.cover: The archdiocese admitted it 'failed to adequately respond and prevent the sexual abuse' of three boys by a priest
cases.d: In June 2015 the Ramsey County Attorney filed six gross misdemeanor child endangerment charges against the archdiocese itself over its handling of priest Curtis Wehmeyer, later imprisoned for abusing three brothers. The charges were dropped on 20 July 2016 after the archdiocese admitted in court papers that it had failed to adequately respond to and prevent the abuse. A December 2015 civil settlement placed the archdiocese under court oversight until February 2020.
cases.cite: Ramsey County Attorney criminal complaint and civil petition, 5 June 2015; settlement and admission, 20 July 2016, as reported by MPR News

cases.n: US Senate inquiry — Olympic movement and the FBI failed to protect athletes (2019)
cases.who: US Olympic Committee; USA Gymnastics; FBI; Michigan State University
cases.victims_note: 260 women and girls said Larry Nassar assaulted them
cases.cover: The report found the USOC and USA Gymnastics concealed their negligence and avoided reform after survivors spoke out, and that the FBI also 'fundamentally failed' to protect gymnasts
cases.d: An 18-month investigation by the Senate Commerce subcommittee led by Senators Jerry Moran and Richard Blumenthal reported on 30 July 2019. It found that the US Olympic Committee, USA Gymnastics and the FBI 'fundamentally failed' to protect gymnasts from Larry Nassar, and that the Olympic bodies concealed their negligence. It found institutions repeatedly failed to refer wrongdoing to law enforcement. The report accompanied proposed legislation to reform oversight of Olympic sport.
cases.cite: US Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Manufacturing, Trade and Consumer Protection, Olympic abuse investigation report, 30 July 2019, as reported by UPI

cases.n: Ropes & Gray report for the US Olympic Committee — Nassar (2018)
cases.who: US Olympic Committee; USA Gymnastics
cases.cover: USA Gymnastics' CEO told the USOC's CEO and chief of sport performance of allegations against Nassar in 2015; neither shared it and the USOC took no action until press reports in September 2016
cases.d: A 233-page report by the law firm Ropes & Gray, commissioned by the US Olympic Committee and released on 10 December 2018, was based on more than 100 interviews over 10 months. It found that in 2015 USA Gymnastics' chief executive told the USOC's chief executive and its chief of sport performance that national team members had alleged abuse by Larry Nassar, and that the USOC took no action from July 2015 until the Indianapolis Star published in September 2016. The USOC fired its chief of sport performance the day the report was released.
cases.cite: Ropes & Gray, Report of the Independent Investigation: The Constellation of Factors Underlying Larry Nassar's Abuse of Athletes, 10 December 2018, as reported by CNN via WTVR

cases.n: Daniels review of USA Gymnastics (2017)
cases.who: USA Gymnastics
cases.cover: Reporting rules were so unclear and poorly enforced that the reviewer described the result as 'inadvertent suppression'
cases.d: Former federal prosecutor Deborah Daniels, commissioned by USA Gymnastics in late 2016 after lawsuits over abuse by coaches and team doctor Larry Nassar, released her review on 27 June 2017. She found reporting protocols unclear and poorly enforced, a culture that put performance ahead of protection, and an opaque process for investigating claims. She made 70 recommendations, which the board adopted unanimously.
cases.cite: Deborah J. Daniels, review for USA Gymnastics, June 2017, as reported by AP / Sports Illustrated, 27 June 2017

cases.n: Justice Department inspector general — FBI mishandling of Nassar allegations (2021)
cases.who: FBI Indianapolis field office; USA Gymnastics
cases.victims_note: At least 40 girls and women said they were abused over a 14-month period while the FBI knew of allegations
cases.cover: FBI Indianapolis officials did not act for months, did not interview two of three athletes, and later gave incomplete and inaccurate information to internal FBI inquiries
cases.d: The Justice Department's Office of the Inspector General reported on 14 July 2021 that the FBI made 'numerous and fundamental errors' after USA Gymnastics reported allegations against Larry Nassar to its Indianapolis office in 2015. Months passed before a formal investigation was opened; agents interviewed only one of three athletes, by phone. Officials later gave incomplete and inaccurate information when their handling was questioned. At least 40 girls and women reported being abused during the 14 months the FBI knew of the allegations.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice Office of the Inspector General, Investigation and Review of the FBI's Handling of Allegations of Sexual Abuse by Former USA Gymnastics Physician Lawrence Gerard Nassar, 14 July 2021, as reported by AP / OPB

cases.n: GAO-11-200 — US schools hired or kept staff with histories of sexual misconduct (2010)
cases.who: Public and private K-12 schools in 11 US states
cases.cover: School officials let teachers resign rather than face discipline and in some cases gave positive references that helped them get jobs at other schools; some schools did no criminal history check
cases.d: The US Government Accountability Office released GAO-11-200 on 16 December 2010 after examining 15 cases in 11 states where schools hired or retained people with histories of sexual misconduct. In at least 11 cases the offenders had previously targeted children and in at least 6 they abused more children after being hired. Officials sometimes allowed resignations instead of discipline and wrote positive references; some schools did no fingerprint-based checks. GAO found no federal law governing the employment of sex offenders in schools.
cases.cite: US Government Accountability Office, GAO-11-200, K-12 Education: Selected Cases of Public and Private Schools That Hired or Retained Individuals with Histories of Sexual Misconduct, December 2010; House Education and Labor Committee release

cases.n: Indian Health Service — Presidential Task Force after pediatrician Stanley Patrick Weber (2020)
cases.place: Pine Ridge, South Dakota (IHS hospital); also Browning, Montana
cases.who: US Indian Health Service (IHS)
cases.cover: After complaints the IHS transferred Weber to another IHS hospital, where he practised for another 21 years; staff did not know their reporting obligations
cases.d: Stanley Patrick Weber, an Indian Health Service pediatrician, was convicted of sexually abusing boys in his care at IHS hospitals in Montana and South Dakota. A White House task force chaired by US Attorney Trent Shores reported on 23 July 2020 that IHS staff did not know their federal duties to report suspected abuse, that the agency sometimes overlooked doctors' troubled histories to fill posts, and that its child-protection policy conflicted in places with federal law. After complaints, the agency had moved Weber to another IHS hospital, where he worked for another 21 years.
cases.cite: Presidential Task Force on Protecting Native American Children in the Indian Health Service System, report, April 2020 (released 23 July 2020), as reported by PBS Frontline

cases.n: Justice Department finds sexual abuse in five Texas juvenile facilities (2024)
cases.place: Gainesville State School and four other TJJD facilities, Texas
cases.who: Texas Juvenile Justice Department (TJJD)
cases.cover: The Justice Department said Texas state agencies and the Texas Rangers had substantiated sexual abuse at TJJD facilities since the early 2000s and the problem persisted
cases.d: On 1 August 2024 the US Justice Department announced findings that the Texas Juvenile Justice Department fails to protect children from sexual abuse by staff and other children at all five of its secure facilities (Evins, Gainesville, Giddings, McLennan County and Ron Jackson), in violation of the Constitution. It also found excessive force, prolonged isolation and inadequate mental-health care. The department noted that state investigations had substantiated sexual abuse at these facilities since the early 2000s.
cases.cite: US Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division findings report on the Texas Juvenile Justice Department, 1 August 2024 (press release)

cases.n: Texas Youth Commission sexual abuse scandal — Rangers report and legislative takeover (2007)
cases.place: West Texas State School, Pyote, Texas
cases.who: Texas Youth Commission (state juvenile corrections)
cases.cover: Complaints at the West Texas State School from 2003 to 2005 were largely ignored; a TYC headquarters inquiry found no abuse; the local district attorney never took the Texas Rangers' case to a grand jury
cases.d: A Texas Ranger's 229-page report documented sexual abuse of boys by two senior administrators at the West Texas State School in Pyote, where complaints from 2003 to 2005 had been ignored and the local prosecutor did not take the case to a grand jury. When this became public in February 2007, investigators counted more than 750 sexual abuse complaints across all 13 Texas Youth Commission facilities from January 2000 to February 2007. The TYC board resigned on 16 March 2007, the Senate approved a conservator for the agency, and by May 2007, 93 employees had been suspended, fired or forced to retire.
cases.cite: Texas Rangers investigative report on the West Texas State School; Texas Senate Criminal Justice Committee actions, 2007, as reported by Prison Legal News, 15 February 2008

cases.n: Law Commission of Canada — 'Restoring Dignity': child abuse in Canadian institutions (2000)
cases.who: Government-run and government-funded institutions for children, including Indian residential schools
cases.d: In November 1997 the federal Minister of Justice asked the Law Commission of Canada to report on processes for dealing with physical and sexual abuse of children in government-run, government-funded and government-sponsored institutions. Its report, Restoring Dignity: Responding to Child Abuse in Canadian Institutions, was presented in March 2000. It reviewed the history of residential schools and other institutions and assessed redress options, recommending programmes negotiated with survivors that avoid causing further harm, together with public education and prevention measures.
cases.cite: Law Commission of Canada, Restoring Dignity: Responding to Child Abuse in Canadian Institutions, March 2000 (Department of Justice Canada archive)

cases.n: Jericho Hill School for the Deaf, Vancouver — Berger special counsel and BC Ombudsman (1992–1993)
cases.who: Jericho Hill Provincial School for the Deaf (BC Ministry of Education)
cases.victims_note: About 300 former students received payments under the 1992 compensation plan
cases.cover: A boy disclosed abuse by a staff member in 1982 and more students came forward in 1987, but no charges followed; the province later fought a class action through the courts before settling
cases.d: A teenage boy disclosed sexual abuse by a counsellor at the provincial school for deaf children in 1982, and more students came forward in 1987. Former judge Thomas Berger, appointed special counsel in 1992, concluded that abuse had occurred, including abuse of younger children by more than 20 older students, and the BC Ombudsman issued Public Report No. 32 on the abuse of deaf students on 8 November 1993. About 300 former students received payments under a 1992 compensation plan, and in 2004 the province committed $15.6 million to settle a class action.
cases.cite: BC Ombudsman, Public Report No. 32: Abuse of Deaf Students at Jericho Hill School, 8 November 1993; The Tyee, 13 April 2004

cases.n: Nova Scotia — Kaufman review of the response to institutional abuse (2002)
cases.who: Nova Scotia provincial youth institutions and the province's compensation programme
cases.victims_note: The compensation programme received 1,264 claims; Kaufman found both that abuse occurred and that there were false and exaggerated claims
cases.d: Retired judge Fred Kaufman, appointed by Nova Scotia's Justice Minister in November 1999, delivered 'Searching for Justice: An Independent Review of Nova Scotia's Response to Reports of Institutional Abuse' on 31 January 2002. The province's compensation programme for people abused in provincial youth institutions had received 1,264 claims and paid about $39 million. Kaufman stated that sexual and physical abuse did occur, but found the programme 'seriously flawed' because claims required little validation, found significant evidence of false and exaggerated claims, and found that staff were branded as abusers without recourse. He made 105 recommendations.
cases.cite: Fred Kaufman, Searching for Justice, 31 January 2002; Nova Scotia government news release; The Irish Times, 9 February 2002

cases.n: Quebec National Assembly special commission on the sexual exploitation of minors (2020)
cases.who: Pimping networks and sex-trade establishments exploiting minors in Quebec
cases.d: A cross-party special commission of Quebec's National Assembly studied the sexual exploitation of minors for 18 months, with hearings in Quebec City, Montreal and Val-d'Or, and tabled its final report on 3 December 2020. It estimated about 600 establishments in Quebec, such as strip clubs, massage parlours and escort agencies, where a man could find a teenager for sex, described Montreal as a national hub, and said pimps could earn up to $300,000 a year. It made 58 recommendations, the first being to make the fight against sexual exploitation of minors a national priority.
cases.cite: Commission spéciale sur l'exploitation sexuelle des mineurs, final report, December 2020, as reported by Global News, 3 December 2020

cases.n: Victoria — 'Betrayal of Trust' parliamentary inquiry into religious and other organisations (2013)
cases.who: Catholic Church and other religious and non-government organisations in Victoria
cases.cover: The inquiry found the Catholic Church's early-1990s response continued to conceal abuse; senior church representatives conceded steps intended to conceal wrongdoing
cases.d: The Family and Community Development Committee of the Parliament of Victoria tabled 'Betrayal of Trust', its report of the Inquiry into the Handling of Child Abuse by Religious and Other Non-Government Organisations, on 13 November 2013. It found 'substantial criminal child abuse' over a long period by priests and members of religious orders in Victoria, and a culture in religious organisations that allowed systemic abuse. It recommended making it a crime for religious leaders and others to fail to report abuse and removing the church's practical immunity from being sued.
cases.cite: Parliament of Victoria Family and Community Development Committee, Betrayal of Trust, 13 November 2013, as reported by The Tablet and The Guardian

cases.n: Wood Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service — paedophile inquiry (1997)
cases.who: A Sydney paedophile network linked to convicted sex offender Colin Fisk; a group of NSW police detectives
cases.cover: The network paid detectives for advance warning of police scrutiny; the Commission found police, prosecutors and public servants had handled sex offences against minors poorly
cases.d: The Royal Commission into the NSW Police Service under Justice James Wood (1994–1997) had its terms widened in 1995 to cover paedophile networks and the protection of at-risk minors; Volume IV of its final report, published in 1997, is the paedophile inquiry. It found a network linked to convicted offender Colin Fisk that distributed child abuse material, procured under-age partners and invested in an under-age male brothel in Surry Hills, and that it had a corrupt relationship with a group of detectives who sold it warnings. The Commission rejected claims of a large ring of prominent professionals protected by senior police for lack of evidence.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into the New South Wales Police Service, Final Report, Volume IV: The Paedophile Inquiry, 1997, as summarised by Wikipedia (citing the report)

cases.n: Senate 'Lost Innocents' — child migrants abused in Australian institutions (2001)
cases.place: Bindoon, Western Australia (Christian Brothers' Boys Town)
cases.who: Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia (Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf, Tardun) and other receiving institutions for British and Maltese child migrants
cases.d: The Senate Community Affairs References Committee tabled 'Lost Innocents: Righting the Record — Report on child migration' in August 2001. Of 207 former child migrants who made submissions, 38 described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described 'systemic criminal sexual assault' and predatory behaviour by a large number of Christian Brothers over a long period.
cases.cite: Senate Community Affairs References Committee, Lost Innocents: Righting the Record, 30 August 2001; summarised in IICSA, Child Migration Programmes investigation report, Part B

cases.n: Senate 'Forgotten Australians' — children in institutional care (2004)
cases.who: Australian orphanages, children's homes, foster care and other out-of-home care run by states, churches and charities
cases.victims_note: At least 500,000 children grew up in out-of-home care in the 20th century; the inquiry received hundreds of accounts of abuse
cases.d: The Senate Community Affairs References Committee published 'Forgotten Australians: A report on Australians who experienced institutional or out-of-home care as children' on 30 August 2004. It estimated that at least 500,000 children grew up in institutional or out-of-home care in the 20th century and received hundreds of accounts of emotional, physical and sexual abuse by carers, other children, visitors and foster families. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologised in Parliament to Forgotten Australians and former child migrants on 16 November 2009.
cases.cite: Senate Community Affairs References Committee, Forgotten Australians, 30 August 2004, as summarised by Wikipedia (citing the report and the 2009 apology)

cases.n: South Australia — Child Protection Systems Royal Commission, 'The Life They Deserve' (2016)
cases.who: Families SA (state child protection agency); carer Shannon McCoole
cases.cover: The inquiry examined how Families SA failed to prevent abuse by a carer it employed
cases.d: Former Supreme Court Justice Margaret Nyland led a two-year royal commission set up after Families SA carer Shannon McCoole was jailed for 35 years for sexual offences against children in state care. Her report, 'The Life They Deserve', was delivered to the Governor on 5 August 2016 with 260 recommendations. It found that children in state care had been harmed both by their families and by the system meant to protect them.
cases.cite: Child Protection Systems Royal Commission, The Life They Deserve, 5 August 2016; SBS News

cases.n: Australian Human Rights Commission — 'Change the Routine', gymnastics review (2021)
cases.who: Gymnastics Australia and the sport of gymnastics in Australia
cases.cover: Complaints of abuse and harm were not adequately addressed and athletes' voices were silenced
cases.d: Gymnastics Australia engaged the Australian Human Rights Commission in August 2020 after repeated abuse claims; the Commission's report 'Change the Routine' was released on 3 May 2021. Drawing on 57 interviews and 138 submissions, it heard of emotional, physical and sexual abuse in a sport whose participants are predominantly young girls, found that complaints were not adequately addressed and that children were not effectively safeguarded, and described a 'win-at-all-costs' culture. It made 12 recommendations, including an apology, which Gymnastics Australia accepted.
cases.cite: Australian Human Rights Commission, Change the Routine: Report on the Independent Review into Gymnastics in Australia, May 2021; SBS News, 3 May 2021

cases.n: Western Australia — St Andrew's Hostel Katanning special inquiry (Blaxell, 2012)
cases.who: St Andrew's Hostel, Katanning (state country high school hostel); warden Dennis McKenna
cases.cover: Most officials who received allegations took no action; the inquiry made adverse findings against a police officer and a local councillor
cases.d: Former judge Peter Blaxell was appointed special inquirer on 22 November 2011 to examine how government agencies and officials responded to allegations of sexual abuse at St Andrew's Hostel, a state-run hostel for rural high-school students. Its warden from 1976 to 1990, Dennis McKenna, was convicted in 1991 of 19 offences against five boys and pleaded guilty in 2011 to 10 more, a total of 29 offences against 11 boys aged 14 to 16. The report, 'How the system and society failed our children', found that most officials took no action on allegations and made adverse findings against one police officer and one local councillor.
cases.cite: Special Inquiry into St Andrew's Hostel, Katanning, report 'St Andrew's Hostel Katanning: How the system and society failed our children', 2012 (Government of Western Australia)

cases.n: Nauru detention centre — Moss Review and Senate inquiry on abuse of asylum-seeker children (2015)
cases.who: Australian-funded Regional Processing Centre on Nauru; contracted guards and staff
cases.cover: Staff wrote in an open letter in April 2015 that the Australian government had known of abuses against women and children for over 18 months
cases.d: The Moss Review, commissioned by the Australian government and reported in March 2015, found it possible that guards at the Australian-run Regional Processing Centre on Nauru had traded marijuana for sexual favours with asylum-seeker children. In April 2015 staff alleged multiple instances of sexual abuse of women and children in an open letter. A Senate select committee reported on 31 August 2015 in 'Taking responsibility: conditions and circumstances at Australia's Regional Processing Centre in Nauru'.
cases.cite: Philip Moss, Review into recent allegations relating to conditions and circumstances at the Regional Processing Centre in Nauru, February 2015 (published March 2015); Senate Select Committee report, 31 August 2015; as summarised by Wikipedia

notes:
Scope of this file: Checklist 1 (major official findings) for the United States and its territories, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and the Pacific. Built from Bishop Accountability's list of US grand jury and attorney-general reports (bishop-accountability.org/AtAGlance/reports.htm, used only as a finding aid; each item is cited to the AG release or a news report), plus Senate/parliament pages, government press releases and major outlets.

Search budget: the shared web-search limit for this turn ran out partway through the Australia/NZ/Pacific work. Items below marked UNCONFIRMED were not researched further for that reason; a follow-up pass can add them.

US gaps and borderline calls:
- Westchester grand jury 2002: number of priests and victims not stated in the source opened; fields left out.
- Philadelphia: the 2003 grand jury's report was made public with the 2005 report and is counted as one item.
- Michigan AG: the six diocesan reports (Marquette 2022, Gaylord 2024, Kalamazoo 2024, Lansing 2024, Grand Rapids 2025, Saginaw 2026) are six checklist items pointing to one new case (x-usa-michigan-ag-diocesan-reports). The Archdiocese of Detroit report (seventh) was not yet published as of the June 2026 release. Counts for Marquette, Gaylord and Kalamazoo were not in the sources opened.
- NY AG Buffalo (lawsuit + 2022 settlement) and Brooklyn (2024 assurance of discontinuance) are AG enforcement actions rather than fact-finding reports; included as 'settled' because they are AG investigations of whole dioceses. Lead may drop them.
- Ramsey County 2015 charges against the Archdiocese of St Paul and Minneapolis are included as a prosecutor action against a whole institution that ended in an admission (status acknowledged).
- Kansas KBI report: the brief's date assumption differs; the source dates coverage to January 2023. The KBI review was requested by the Archbishop of Kansas City in Kansas.
- No published state report found (as of sources opened) for: Louisiana (Louisiana State Police / FBI investigation of the Archdiocese of New Orleans, reported in 2024 as a child sex-trafficking inquiry; no report located), New Mexico and New Jersey (Bishop Accountability says reports are being prepared, none released), Wisconsin, Virginia, Washington, Delaware. Cuyahoga County (Cleveland) 2002 investigation of 145 clergy was never published (excluded).
- Ohio State (Strauss) and University of Michigan (Anderson) excluded: victims overwhelmingly adult students. University of Southern California (Tyndall) not listed for the same reason. Michigan State and Penn State are covered by usa-nassar and usa-penn-state-sandusky.
- USA Swimming: no official or commissioned report found; existing case stays as 'reported'.
- Senate Olympic report 2019: title not given in the source opened; the item is named by committee.
- Texas Youth Commission 2007: the two West Texas State School administrators were indicted (not named in the case text because the source opened gives charges, not verdicts).
- New net key used: none created. Gymnastics cases use existing net 'usa-gymnastics'; Lost Innocents uses 'uk-child-migration'; Restoring Dignity uses 'canada-residential-schools'.

Canada:
- Jericho Hill: Berger (1992 special counsel) and BC Ombudsman Public Report No. 32 (8 Nov 1993) are combined into one item. Victim count comes from compensation numbers (~300).
- Excluded borderline: MMIWG National Inquiry 2019 (violence against Indigenous women and girls; child trafficking a minor part), Indian Day Schools settlement (settlement, not a finding), Sixties Scoop (removal-only scope), CCCB 'From Pain to Hope' (guidelines). Safe-sport findings (Heritage committee 2024; Future of Sport in Canada Commission final report 24 March 2026) excluded only because the sources opened did not state findings on sexual abuse of minors — worth verifying.
- UNCONFIRMED / not researched: Hockey Canada and Graham James (no official inquiry into child abuse found; the 2022 Commons hearings concerned an alleged assault of an adult). Ontario Christian Brothers training schools (St. Joseph's, St. John's) 1990s compensation agreement. Archdiocese of Montreal reviews (Capriolo 2020, Denis audit) are diocesan-commissioned and would fail rule 1.

Australia:
- Royal Commission counted once (aus-royal-commission-final). Its case studies already on the map are not listed as separate checklist items.
- Betrayal of Trust: victim and offender figures not in the sources opened.
- Wood Royal Commission: cited via Wikipedia's summary of Volume IV (the LECC report PDFs appeared in search results but were not opened).
- Katanning: report date is 2012 (references run through May 2012); exact month not in the visible text.
- Excluded borderline (lead may add): Little Children are Sacred (NT 2007) and the Mullighan APY Lands inquiry (SA 2008, 141 children, including girls trading sex for petrol or drugs) — both community abuse rather than institutions or networks. DART / DLA Piper review: minors not confirmed in source opened.
- UNCONFIRMED / not researched (search limit): Victoria's Board of Inquiry into historical child sexual abuse in Beaumaris Primary School and other government schools (2024); Queensland CMC inquiry into abuse of children in foster care ('Protecting Children', 2004); Tasmanian Ombudsman review of claims of abuse in state care (2004); WA Gordon Inquiry (2002); SA Debelle inquiry (2013); Anglican Church of Australia-commissioned Parkinson study (2009; source URL blocked); Australian Human Rights Commission 'Forgotten Children' (immigration detention, 2014).

New Zealand:
- Abuse in Care Royal Commission counted once (final report), plus its named institutional reports already on the map (Lake Alice, Marylands, Catholic findings).
- UNCONFIRMED / not researched: Confidential Listening and Assistance Service final report (2015). Dilworth inquiry excluded (school-commissioned).

Pacific:
- Nauru: Moss Review (2015) and Senate select committee (2015) added as one case (x-nru-nauru-rpc-2015); no child victim count in the source opened. The 2016 'Nauru Files' leak (press) not added.
- No official finding meeting the checklist rules was found for Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Samoa (other than the US Focus on Children prosecution), Tonga, Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Micronesia, Palau or Northern Mariana Islands. Leads not researched (search limit): Solomon Islands logging-camp sexual exploitation of girls (government and church reports), Kiribati sexual exploitation of girls by foreign fishing crews (UNICEF/Kiribati government study), Diocese of Chalan Kanoa (CNMI) bankruptcy. Guam is covered by gum-apuron-agana.
